schools.summary: Gill: God rebukes his own only in love, never in wrath, though they fear otherwise; Calvin: David owns the stroke as the just recompense of sin, doubts a bodily disease is in view, and asks only not to be dealt with in strict justice.

Keil and Delitzsch trace three strophes from distress to confidence and, finding no confession of sin, question the psalm's place among the penitential seven; Ellicott says the discipline-of-love thought is checked by the sufferer's praying for the chastisement to be altogether removed (cf. Ps. 38:1).

Henry: the prayer is not 'rebuke me not' but 'not in thine anger,' the body's ache tolerable if the heart be spared; Spurgeon: folly to pray against the golden hand, only that the rod not become a sword.
Clarke: the inscription (Neginoth, Sheminith = eight strings) is uncertain; the psalm is the first of the seven Penitential Psalms, written under a grievous disease after the sin with Bathsheba.
Augustine reads the title's 'eighth' as the day of judgment, the world's seven millennia as seven days and the eighth the age to come, yet warns that no man may compute that day.

debates.question: What is the affliction behind the psalm?

sides.position: a bodily disease, sent after the sin with Bathsheba
not necessarily a disease but some severe calamity; 'weak' used metaphorically

debates.question: Does the deprecation ask only that the anger be removed, or the chastening itself?

sides.position: only the anger and hot displeasure are deprecated; the chastening itself is accepted
the context shows the sufferer praying for the chastisement to be altogether removed

outliers.note: Reads the obscure title 'of the eighth' eschatologically, of the day of judgment after the world's seven thousand years, while cautioning that the day cannot be reckoned by any computation of years.
Because the psalm contains no confession of sin, doubts whether the church rightly numbered it the first of the seven penitential psalms.

themes: the first of the seven Penitential Psalms

schools.summary: Gill: David pleads no merit and no former righteousness, but flings himself wholly on the mercy of God in Christ.
Henry on a stricken king: great men are men, and neither strength nor goodness keeps the saints from sickness ('he whom thou lovest is sick').
Clarke: 'I have no merit'; no earthly physician can cure a malady of body and soul together; 'weak' an utter exhaustion, the disease entered into the bones.

Ellicott: 'weak' properly to wither or languish (Hos. 4:3; Isa. 16:8), 'vexed' literally 'affrighted' (LXX, Vulgate); Keil and Delitzsch: the plea founded on the yearning to praise God, God to rescue the soul on the ground of his mercy to sinners.

themes: have mercy for I am weak
heal me, my bones are vexed
no merit but mercy in Christ
to wither or to be affrighted

schools.summary: Gill: the soul sore vexed by indwelling sin and transgression, the hidings of God's face, the temptations of Satan, and the fear of death.
Clarke reads the unfinished cry as the impatience of pain: 'how long before thou speak peace to my troubled heart?'
Ellicott: the broken 'how long?' (cf. Ps. 90:13) is 'belief in unbelief' (Domine quousque, Calvin's motto), the church's faith amid despair also heard in Zech. 1:12 and Rev. 6:10.
Henry: the trouble was long as well as sharp; at such a time we must turn to the living God, the only physician of body and mind, not to the Assyrians or the god of Ekron.
Gill: God being omnipresent, 'return' is not properly ascribed to him; he departs as to sensible communion and hides his face, returning when he manifests his favour again.
Clarke: the word confesses a backslider; awful to be forced to say 'Return,' yet mercy that a backslider may return and expect God to return to him.
Keil and Delitzsch: the accent of the Hebrew 'return' thrown onto the last syllable; God has turned away, and the whole prayer is that he turn back and save on the ground of his mercy.
Henry: the sum of the psalmist's desires, that God receive him into favour and preserve the inward man, delivering the soul from sinning, sinking, and perishing, all 'for thy mercies' sake.'
Gill: a dead man can make no mention of God's works and is useless to the living; Calvin: David regrets that being taken from the world would rob him of the chance to praise God.
Clarke: man is made to glorify God on earth, an end the grave cannot serve; Wesley: 'remembrance' is the public celebration of grace in the land of the living, not the work of the other life.
Ellicott: the plea from the loss God's praise would suffer (Ps. 30:9; Isa. 38:18); sheol a magnified grave where the rephaim 'know not anything,' the undeveloped picture arguing against a late date.
Henry: two senses (the second death's blaspheming, and the body's ended service); soldiers in the field more useful than courtiers, to abide in the flesh more profitable for the church.

outliers.note: Builds a long excursus on sheol as a magnified grave, the rephaim weak shadowy existences less alive even than Homer's shades, and makes the psalm's undeveloped doctrine of the dead an argument against a late date.

themes: praising God in the land of the living

schools.summary: Gill: weary of his very groaning, whose many springs are sin, wrath, Satan, and the fear of death; inward groaning wastes the spirits and consumes the flesh.
Ellicott: the drenched couch echoes Homer's Odyssey; Easterns vent freely a grief the colder West is trained to hide.
Wesley: it becomes the greatest spirits to relent under God's displeasure; David who could face Goliath melts into tears, with no diminution to his character.
Henry: true penitents weep in secret, unlike the Pharisees who mourned to be seen; sorrow for sin ought to be great sorrow.
Gill: the word carries anger and the sorrow that rises from it; grief, whether indignation at foes or the sense of wrath, vents in tears that weaken and dim the eye.
Clarke renders the eye 'blasted, withered, sunk in my head.'
Ellicott: 'consumed' is sunken, fallen away, the same word as 'vexed' in v.2; grief brings the marks of premature age (Job 17:7; Ps. 31:9).
Henry: the eye waxed old 'because of enemies' who rejoiced and misread his tears; the triumphs of the wicked add much to the grief of saints.

Gill: a quick passage from a gloomy frame to a comfortable one; the 'workers of iniquity' are open foes or secret courtiers, among whom God's people must dwell (Lot, David in Meshech, the lily among thorns).

Henry: the man newly sure his lot is among the chosen dismisses the taunting enemies (words the Lord borrows, Luke 13:27), for 'silent tears are not speechless ones'; Spurgeon: joy comes in the morning, the pardoned soul sweeps out the wicked, weeping the eloquence of sorrow understood in heaven.
Clarke: the enemies upbraided him to drive him to despair, but the Lord forgave his sins; Wesley: by the workings of grace on his heart he knew his prayer accepted, his tears cries to God.

Ellicott: the morning of revived faith after the night of sorrow; Keil and Delitzsch: even before the plaint ends the light breaks in, confidence flashing thrice, 'hath heard' the fact and acceptance its consequence.

themes: depart from me, ye workers of iniquity
the Lord hath heard the voice of my weeping

schools.summary: Gill: the 'supplication' sums all the psalmist had poured out; petitions for grace and mercy offered under the Spirit of grace and supplication, now heard.
Keil and Delitzsch: the two tenses set side by side, 'hath heard' stating the accomplished fact and 'will receive' drawing out its consequence.
Henry: 'he has heard... and therefore he will receive my prayer; for he gives, and does not upbraid'; from this one hearing he infers the audience of all his prayers.

themes: the LORD hath heard my supplication

schools.summary: Clarke: 'may they be suddenly converted,' the sense most congenial to Christian principles; Wesley: ashamed of their vain confidence, and 'returning' in repentance to their obedience.
Gill: the clause a prophecy, or a wish that no real ill befall them but that the unashamed be brought to repentance, or shamed hereafter before the Judge of quick and dead.
Ellicott: not conversion but rout; 'return' means to retire discomfited and in failure, as Milton rendered it.
Henry: either a prayer for their penitence or a prediction of their ruin, the evil they wished returning on their own heads (cf. v.3).

debates.question: Are the psalm's closing words a sentence of ruin on the enemies or a prayer for their conversion?

sides.position: a prayer for their repentance and conversion
a prediction of their discomfiture and rout
left open — either their conversion or, failing that, their ruin
